fixes.explanation: Ditch the tents? Then we're all standing in a field with nowhere to put the family, friend. That's not the plan. Jacob tells his household and all who were with him to get rid of “…the foreign gods that are among you.” Tents can come along to Bethel. The other gods can't.

That's it, friend! The household hands Jacob “…all their foreign gods and all their earrings…” (Genesis 35:4). Picture him standing there with his arms getting fuller and fuller. Then he buries the whole pile under the oak near Shechem, and they're ready to head for Bethel.

Sandals are a good guess, friend, but that's not the word in this verse. The household hands Jacob “…all their foreign gods and all their earrings…” Earrings is your blank. Then Jacob buries the whole pile under the oak near Shechem.

Staffs, friend? I can see why you'd reach for that one, but it's not in this verse. The household gives Jacob “…all their foreign gods and all their earrings…” Earrings is the blank. Then Jacob buries the lot under the oak near Shechem. I once stamped a whole batch before I checked the recipe, so I get it.

A storm is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word here. The verse says, “…a terror from God fell over the surrounding cities, so that they did not pursue Jacob’s sons.” It came from God, and it fell on the cities around them. That's why nobody chased Jacob's family.

problems.problem: The joke says getting rid of the tents would make the trip short, but the image of sleeping under the open sky does not explain why the trip would be short.
The explanation is flat and repetitive: it quotes what they gave Jacob, then restates that the pile went to him without adding much personality.
The text does not say the household had sandals or kept them on their feet.
The text does not say the household had staffs or kept them in hand.
“A wrong answer there too” calls the baker’s answer wrong, which Papa does not do.
“No clouds, no thunder” asserts weather details the passage does not give.
